items.title: The Himalayas: A Natural Barrier and Water Tower
items.explanation: The Himalayan Mountain range forms a massive wall in the north of India, separating it from Nepal, Bhutan, China, Pakistan, and Afghanistan. It is approximately 2500 km long. Its peaks are over 8000 meters high, making them part of the 'Eight Thousanders'. The range acts as a crucial barrier shaping India's climate and culture. It is also known as the 'Water Tower of Asia' because melting snow feeds major rivers like the Ganga, Indus, and Brahmaputra.

items.title: Formation of the Himalayas
items.explanation: About 50 million years ago, India broke away from Gondwana (Africa) and collided with Eurasia. This collision caused the land between them to crumple and rise, forming the mighty Himalayan mountains. Today, India continues to push into Asia at a slow rate of about five centimeters per year.

items.title: Sacred Mountains and Rivers
items.explanation: The Himalayas are considered sacred by many cultures. Temples and monasteries have been built within them, attracting spiritual seekers. The Ganga River originates from the Gaumukh (Cow's Mouth) in Uttarakhand, where the Bhagirathi River also flows. These rivers provide essential water for drinking, farming, and industry.
